hook.say: before the story, can i ask you something? who do you live or work most closely with right now?
options: then you know how hard and how good it can be. listen.
then this one’s for you. listen.
then listen for what a few good friends can be.

steps.line: Three monks lived together in a quiet forest grove. One day the Buddha came to visit, and asked one of them, Anuruddha, how they were getting on.
“Do you live in harmony,” he asked, “blending like milk and water, looking at each other with kind eyes?”

steps.q: Living so close in the forest, how do you think they keep the peace?
o: Each sets aside his own wishes for theirs
They agree on rules and stick to them
They give each other plenty of space
steps.why: Each one quietly sets aside what he wants, for the others. Not rules, not distance.

steps.line: “I think, how lucky I am to live with friends like these,” Anuruddha said. “So I set aside what I want, and do what they want.”

steps.q: Anuruddha says he’s kind to his friends in deed, word and thought, “openly and in private.” Why might “in private” matter?
o: Kindness that needs an audience isn’t real
Monks weren’t allowed to praise each other aloud
Private kindness was said to earn more merit
steps.why: In the sutta (MN 31) he keeps up kindness toward them even when they can’t see. Care that doesn’t need credit is the kind that lasts.

steps.line: Whoever saw the water pot empty filled it. If it was too heavy, he waved a friend over, and they lifted it together, without a word.
And every fifth night they sat up together, talking about the teaching. “We are different in body,” Anuruddha said, “but one in mind.”

steps.q: Three different people, and Anuruddha says they’re “one in mind.” From the story, how did they get there?
o: By choosing each other’s wishes, daily
The Buddha set them one shared goal
steps.why: The sutta tells it as practice, not luck: kind deeds, words and thoughts, day after day, until three minds moved as one.

steps.q: If the water pot was too heavy, the sutta says they called a friend with a wave of the hand. Why not just call out?
o: Calling out would disturb the Buddha
Their voices didn’t carry in the forest
They didn’t break their silence for chores
steps.why: Anuruddha tells the Buddha they don’t break into speech over a water pot. Small chores, done quietly, kept their minds free for practice.

steps.line: Today, a shared kitchen. Somebody always refills the water jug, and nobody sees who. In the old word, that small refill is sangha.
steps.label: today

say: sangha means a community. it’s the third of buddhism’s three jewels: the buddha, the teaching, and the people who practice it. ananda once said good friends are half the holy life. the buddha answered: not half. the whole of it.

in theravada countries, sangha usually means the monks and nuns. in japan, many temple priests marry and raise families. and many western buddhists use sangha for any group that sits together, even online.

steps.q: The Buddha asked how they lived, and the answer was chores. What does that suggest about real community?
o: It comes from people who think alike
It’s built from small, unseen kindnesses
It needs clear rules everyone agrees on
steps.why: Not speeches. Water pots. Small care, given without being asked, is what the Buddha heard as harmony.

today.say: today, do one small unseen thing for the people you live or work with: refill the jug, wash the extra cup, take out the bin. don’t mention it. that’s how three monks kept a forest in harmony.
options: i believe you. today, notice who does it for you.
